sources.title: Italian A1 reference syllabus (four certifying bodies)

units.title: Make first contact
units.description: Greet, exchange names, and choose familiar or polite address.

lessons.title: Begin and end an exchange
lessons.outcome: I can greet someone and take leave.
lessons.takeaway: Ciao is familiar; buongiorno is a polite greeting; arrivederci ends an exchange.

Sara: “My name is Sara. And you?”
Luca: “My name is Luca.”

lessons.title: Thank and ask politely
lessons.outcome: I can use grazie, prego, scusi and per favore in their different jobs.
lessons.takeaway: Grazie thanks someone; prego responds; scusi gets attention; per favore softens a request.

targets.label: Thank and ask politely
targets.explanation: Grazie thanks someone; prego responds; scusi gets attention; per favore softens a request.

repair.title: Try thank and ask politely again
repair.body: Grazie thanks someone. Prego is a natural answer to thanks.

steps.body: Listen and read these before answering.

steps.title: Thank and answer
steps.body: Grazie thanks someone. Prego is a natural answer to thanks.

steps.title: Get attention
steps.body: Scusi attracts attention politely. Per favore belongs inside a request.

steps.translation: Someone thanks you; answer “You are welcome.”
steps.explanation: Prego answers grazie.
steps.hint: This is a reply to thanks.

steps.title: A small favour
steps.it:
Luca: «Scusi. Un caffè, per favore.»
Barista: «Ecco il caffè.»
Luca: «Grazie!»
Barista: «Prego!»
steps.en:
Luca: “Excuse me. A coffee, please.”
Barista: “Here is the coffee.”
Luca: “Thank you!”
Barista: “You are welcome!”
steps.task: Notice how the taught expression works in this short exchange.

lessons.title: Read two c patterns
lessons.outcome: I can connect familiar c spellings with their taught sounds.
lessons.takeaway: C before a or o is hard in casa and come. C before e is soft in cena. In ciao the i signals soft c but is not a separate vowel sound.

targets.label: Read two c patterns
targets.explanation: C before a or o is hard in casa and come. C before e is soft in cena. In ciao the i signals soft c but is not a separate vowel sound.

steps.title: The h keeps the sound hard
steps.body: Before e or i, c normally has the soft sound heard in cena. Add h to keep the hard sound: che, chi, chilo and chiesa. The h is a spelling signal; it is not a separate sound.
